title: We challenged ourselves to build a mystery game in 3 months. It was our first project together, and here's what we learned
author: UndeadGames-studio
selftext:
It was just three of us, three months, and our first real project as a team. One of us is the artist and lead writer, one is the developer, and one runs the project and the funding. We built the game with heavy help from AI (Claude code Opus and Sonnet and OpenAI's codex).

Our game PARALLAX is a mystery RPG you play entirely on a fictional smartphone. You broke your leg and you're stuck at home, so your phone is your only window into the town. Your 19-year-old cousin does the legwork, and you direct him by chat: "Go check the riverbank." "Take a photo." (He's scared, so you have to talk him into it.) There's no map and no movement, just conversation and delegation.

What we learned

1. AI builds fast, and that makes you think you're further along than you are. In August, AI helped us build almost the entire game in a matter of days: the phone interface, the simulated town, and two complete storylines. It felt finished. Then testers rated it 5/10, lower than our rough first prototype. While building so much so quickly, the AI had quietly left out things the prototype already did well. After that we made a rule: a new version has to do everything the old one did before we add anything new
2. Our AI testers were cheating without meaning to. To test the game quickly, we had AI "players" with different personalities play through it. The scores looked great. Then we noticed a bug in our setup: the testers could see hidden information behind the scenes, including hints about the solutions. They weren't solving the mystery, they were reading the answer key. Every score up to that point was useless. Since then we test with friends. That's much slower, and you never know if they'll play long enough to reach the interesting parts, but at least the results are real
3. "Fixed" doesn't mean fixed until you've watched it work. Several times, we (or the AI) said a bug was fixed, and it wasn't. One fix was waiting for a signal the game never sends, so it could never kick in. Another fix was made in the tool that builds the game's content, but we forgot to run that tool, so the fix never made it into the game. We made that second mistake twice
4. Players loved the characters, and hated missing the big moments. Testers loved the characters: one rated them 9/10 while giving the rest of the game 5/10. But five out of thirteen testers named the same frustrating moment on their own. They spent a whole in-game week preparing for a big event, and then only read about it afterwards on social media, like a stranger. One tester had cooked and packed food for a town celebration, and then missed it. Since the player is stuck at home, we couldn't just let them walk there. So now the event comes to you: when something big happens, your phone floods with voice messages, photos, and calls from people who are there
5. Characters feel more real when the AI isn't in charge. In PARALLAX, you can tell characters things, including lies. At first, the AI decided whether a character believed you, and it was too easily convinced. Now the game itself decides, based on how much the character trusts you, what evidence you have, and where your information comes from. The AI only has to put the reaction into words. The characters became much more consistent and believable
6. AI gives you quantity. Humans have to provide quality. The AI wrote 34 documents for the town's archive, and they all sounded the same. Our writer replaced them with 24 handwritten ones that actually feel like they come from one place. Some of her late-night playtest notes turned into real game mechanics. Our project manager decided when something counted as done and what had to be cut. With a 3-month deadline, that job mattered more than we expected
7. Some work AI can't speed up. Getting the game onto Android, translating it into English, making sure the servers could handle players, and publishing on the Play Store still took weeks.

Now PARALLAX is in the final playtest, with an English version and an Android build. We plan to finish the project and use what we learned to start with our passion projects.
